Learn more Build your reading streak0/3 today·Counts at 25% Congo began vaccinating health and other frontline workers against Ebola on Saturday in Bunia, the epicentre of the fastest-growing outbreak of the disease in the country's history, as government figures put the death toll at 3,639. Health authorities are prioritising frontline workers for the Ervebo vaccine, which proved effective in previous outbreaks caused by the more common Zaire strain of the virus. The initial rollout targets the Bunia and Mongbwalu health zones in Ituri province, both among the areas hardest hit by the current epidemic, authorities said on Saturday. Nikole Landu, a healthcare worker who received a dose, said she sought vaccination because she is in constant contact with sick people and at high risk of catching the disease. "So the vaccine I received today will help protect me. I might still get the disease, but I'm less likely to develop a severe case," she said. A vaccine built for a different virus The campaign's central scientific question is whether Ervebo works against the virus now circulating. The vaccine proved effective against Zaire ebolavirus, the strain behind most past outbreaks. Health authorities said it could offer some protection against the Bundibugyo virus driving the current epidemic because the two viruses are related, but whether it actually prevents illness in people infected with Bundibugyo Ebola is still being studied. Because of that uncertainty, the vaccine is being deployed under a compassionate-use program, an arrangement that allows a medical product to be used in a serious disease situation even though it has not been specifically approved for that particular use. The approach trades certainty for speed: instead of waiting for strain-specific evidence, authorities are deploying the vaccine while studies assess whether it works. The campaign will therefore double as a real-world evaluation of cross-protection, with results shaping whether the effort is expanded or reconsidered. The outbreak at a glance As of Saturday, the country had recorded 7,541 confirmed cases, including 3,639 deaths, according to government figures. The outbreak is concentrated in Ituri province, and it is already the deadliest of the 17 Ebola outbreaks recorded in the country. Dividing the reported deaths by confirmed cases yields a case-fatality ratio of roughly 48 percent, a Streamline calculation based on the government figures; the true ratio may differ because the count excludes probable and suspected cases. Key figures for the Ebola outbreak, Ituri province, Democratic Republic of Congo Measure Value Status and source Confirmed cases 7,541 Government figures as of Saturday, reported September 20, 2026 Confirmed deaths 3,639 Government figures as of Saturday, reported September 20, 2026 Case-fatality ratio among confirmed cases About 48 percent Streamline calculation from government figures; excludes probable and suspected cases Outbreak rank Deadliest of 17 in the country Health authorities 2014-2016 West Africa comparison More than 11,000 deaths Deadliest Ebola outbreak on record, mainly Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone The World Health Organization has said the outbreak remains out of control and is on track to surpass the 2014-2016 West Africa epidemic, the deadliest on record, which killed more than 11,000 people, primarily in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone. That projection is a warning rather than an outcome: the Ituri toll is still well below the West African one, and the trajectory will depend on how quickly vaccination, case-finding and treatment can gain ground. Delivery under pressure The rollout begins amid what health authorities describe as extremely difficult conditions, fueled by insecurity, displacement, a health workers' strike and intense population movements. Each factor works against containment: displacement and constant movement raise the risk that infections surface far from treatment, insecurity makes it harder for response teams to reach affected communities, and the strike involves the same healthcare workforce the campaign depends on to run vaccination sites and trace contacts. The choice of who gets vaccinated first reflects that arithmetic. Frontline workers face the highest exposure because they treat patients, which is why authorities put them ahead of the wider population. Their protection also matters for the response itself: an unprotected workforce cannot safely staff treatment centres, and further deaths among health workers would deepen a staffing strain already worsened by industrial action. What to watch The immediate test is delivery: whether doses reach frontline workers across the Bunia and Mongbwalu zones quickly enough to blunt transmission in the epidemic's fastest-moving areas. The decisive unknown is scientific. Whether Ervebo prevents illness in people infected with the Bundibugyo virus remains under study, and the answer will determine how much confidence the effort can claim. For now, the country's deadliest Ebola epidemic has a vaccination campaign in its epicentre, one whose effectiveness is hoped for rather than proven. How did this story land? No sign-in required. OffOn Stream on Scientists warn of weakening health systems and urge stronger outbreak detection West African laboratory scientists are urging governments to strengthen their capacity to detect disease outbreaks to prevent another major crisis ByERICK KAGLAN Associated Press September 18, 2026, 10:38 PM LOME, Togo -- LOME, Togo (AP) — West African laboratory scientists called on governments Friday to strengthen capacity to detect disease outbreaks to avoid another major outbreak, saying health systems across the region are becoming weaker. The scientists issued their warning in Togo's capital, Lome, where they have gathered this week to discuss the region's level of preparation for disease outbreaks and dependence on vaccines from Western countries. They said governments in the region have to cooperate to strengthen disease detection and invest in diagnostic capacities, citing lessons from Ebola and COVID-19 outbreaks that the region has grappled with in the past decade. Between 2014 and 2016, an Ebola outbreak killed at least 11,000 people across West Africa, overwhelmingly in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone. “We need to anticipate these outbreaks,” said Kossi Kabo, the head of the Association of Medical Biologists of Togo and a co-chair of the congress. “We shouldn’t wait for an epidemic to emerge somewhere before responding. By then, it would be too late.” Popular Reads Strait of Hormuz shut until Tehran's conditions met, Ghalibaf says Sep 20 Cindy Crawford's son Presley Gerber dies at 27 2 days ago Twin sisters conjoined at head underwent successful separation surgery: Hospital Sep 16 Africa as a whole remains at risk for outbreaks. The rare Bundibugyo virus has killed over 3,600 people among nearly 7,500 cases in Congo since mid-May, when Congolese authorities announced a fresh deadly Ebola outbreak. The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said the tolls are likely three times the official figures and the outbreak is already history's fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak. The virus spread without detection for several weeks. Also, Hantavirus was detected on a cruise ship that docked in the Atlantic off Cape Verde in May. Scientists are worried that in the absence of a major outbreak threatening the region, maintenance of the health systems has waned, leaving them unprepared for potential future epidemics. Arthur Bodurie Calvin Garber, president of the Sierra Leone Association of Medical Laboratory Scientists, said the governments must also invest in people as much as infrastructure. Britannica Editors Last updated Sep. 19, 2026 •History Britannica AI Ask Anything Table of Contents Table of Contents Ask Anything Viewed through an electron microscope, ebolaviruses appear as long filaments, sometimes branched or intertwined. The virion (virus particle) contains one molecule of noninfectious single-stranded RNA (ribonucleic acid). It is not known how the viruses attack cells; it has been postulated that they produce proteins that suppress the immune system, allowing reproduction of virus to continue unhindered. Viral hemorrhagic fevers similar to Ebola typically are carried by arthropods and rodents, but the natural reservoirs for ebolaviruses are yet to be discovered. Among the suspected reservoirs for Ebola are bats, primates, rodents, and insects that inhabit tropical forests in Africa and Asia. Ebola can be transmitted through contact with infected blood and bodily fluids as well as through contact with surfaces or objects contaminated by those fluids. The virus has also been detected in the organs of patients after recovery from the fever. In men, the virus may remain infectious in semen for as long as two months following return to health. Unsanitary conditions and lack of adequate medical supplies may be factors in the spread of the disease. Burial rituals that involve close contact with the body of a person who has died from the disease also can result in the spread of Ebola. The surfaces of bodies of deceased victims remain infectious for more than a week. In addition, a small percentage of Ebola-infected individuals may remain asymptomatic; such persons may unknowingly carry and spread the virus. Ebolaviruses have an incubation period of 2 to 21 days. The onset of illness is sudden and harsh. Infected persons may develop fever, severe headaches and muscle aches, and loss of appetite. Within a few days the virus causes a condition known as disseminated intravascular coagulation, which is marked by both blood clots and hemorrhaging. In the case of Ebola, clots are concentrated in the liver, spleen, brain, and other internal organs, forcing capillaries to bleed into surrounding tissue. Nausea, vomiting and diarrhea with blood and mucus, conjunctivitis, and sore throat soon follow. A maculopapular rash (discolored elevations of the skin) appears on the trunk and quickly spreads to the limbs and head. The patient is then beset by spontaneous bleeding from body orifices and any breaks in the skin, such as injection sites, and within the gastrointestinal tract, skin, and internal organs. Death is usually brought on by hemorrhaging, shock, or renal failure and occurs within 8 to 17 days. Persons who survive Ebola infection may experience post-Ebola syndrome, symptoms of which include vision problems (potentially blindness), headaches, severe joint and muscle pain, and extreme fatigue. Treatment Treatment for Ebola is primarily with supportive care, including fluids, electrolytes, and medications to stabilize blood pressure and manage complications. Early treatment greatly improves survival. For infections caused by the Zaire strain of Ebola virus, targeted antibody therapies such as REGN-EB3 (Inmazeb) and mAb114 (Ebanga) can help reduce mortality. Other treatments that had been investigated for Ebola included the antiviral drug remdesivir (RDV) and ZMapp, a mixture of three antibodies that bind to proteins on ebolaviruses. ZMapp was administered to infected individuals during the 2014–16 outbreak, though its effectiveness was unclear. In trials during the 2018–20 Ebola outbreak, both REGN-EB3 and mAb114 were found to be more effective at reducing Ebola-related mortality compared with RDV and ZMapp. REGN-EB3 and mAb114 were approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 2020. Ebola virus disease; hand washingA Liberian nurse washing his hands with water after treating a patient sick with Ebola virus disease in Monrovia, Liberia, during the 2014–15 outbreak.(more) The spread of ebolaviruses can be contained by barrier nursing, handling of infected blood and tissue in isolated laboratory units, and proper decontamination of reusable equipment. Experimental vaccines are under development for Ebola, including a vaccine known as VSV-EBOV, which was found to be highly effective in preventing the spread of ebolavirus among persons in close contact with infected individuals. VSV-EBOV was a recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV)-based vaccine that expressed an EBOV glycoprotein. When VSV-EBOV was injected, the vaccinated individuals generated antibodies against the EBOV protein, thereby gaining immunity. Survivors of Ebola infection may be affected by a constellation of long-term health complications known as post-Ebola syndrome. In follow-up studies of persons who recovered from acute Ebola infection, many were found to suffer from uveitis (eye redness and pain), vision loss, tinnitus, hearing loss, stroke, headaches, muscle and joint pain, and other abnormalities in musculoskeletal and neurological function. Some affected individuals also suffered renal failure and were at increased risk of premature death. Post-Ebola syndrome is treated primarily by symptom management with drugs such as analgesics (pain relievers) and anti-inflammatory agents. Viral hemorrhagic fevers (VHFs) are a group of severe illnesses characterized by bleeding, fever, and shock. These diseases are caused by viruses from four families: Flaviviridae, Arenaviridae, Bunyaviridae, and Filoviridae. Flaviviruses Dengue and yellow fever viruses, often transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, are the most common causes. While yellow fever affects the liver and causes severe bleeding, dengue induces only minor bleeding but can result in dengue shock syndrome. Arenaviruses are spread to humans through contact with food or soil contaminated by rodent excreta. This family of viruses causes Lassa fever, Argentine hemorrhagic fever, Bolivian hemorrhagic fever, Brazilian hemorrhagic fever, and Venezuelan hemorrhagic fever. Bunyaviridae includes Hantaviruses, Rift Valley fever virus, and Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus. Hantaviruses are transmitted to humans through rodent contact, while Rift Valley fever is a mosquito-borne disease. Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever is a tick-borne disease. Filoviruses such as Ebola virus and Marburg virus, are highly fatal and may also cause disease in primates. Viral hemorrhagic fevers (VHFs) are a group of highly dangerous illnesses caused by bloodborne viruses that harm the vascular system, resulting in significant bleeding. Initial symptoms include fever, fatigue, and muscle aches. The viruses attack cells and may suppress the immune system, which allows the virus to reproduce. Disseminated intravascular coagulation, a condition marked by blood clots and hemorrhaging, can occur. Clots concentrated in organs force capillaries to bleed into surrounding tissue. This leads to bleeding from body openings, the gastrointestinal tract, skin, and internal organs. Viral hemorrhagic fevers (VHFs) are a group of illnesses caused by bloodborne viruses that damage the vascular system. This damage leads to bleeding under the skin, in internal organs, and from body orifices. Several factors contribute to the ease of bleeding and bruising: * Vascular Damage VHFs can cause vascular damage. * Coagulation Abnormalities Viral infections can cause abnormalities in blood clotting. * Cytokine Release Unregulated cytokine production may lead to vascular damage and hemorrhaging. Some VHFs are highly fatal; certain Ebola strains have mortality rates of up to 90%. Viral hemorrhagic fevers are a group of severe illnesses caused by various virus families that damage the vascular system, leading to bleeding. The body's response involves several complex mechanisms. The infection typically begins with the virus entering the body through contact with an infected animal or insect. Once inside, the virus targets cells in the vascular system, such as endothelial cells, which line blood vessels. The damage to these cells leads to increased vascular permeability and impaired blood clotting. This results in both internal and external hemorrhaging, as blood leaks from the vessels. The immune system responds by releasing cytokines, which are signaling molecules that help coordinate the immune response. However, in severe cases, this can lead to a "cytokine storm," where an excessive amount of cytokines are released, causing inflammation, shock, and organ failure. 2 Britannica Sources viral hemorrhagic fever bloodborne disease: Common bloodborne diseases This answer is created from Britannica articles using AI. Show more Show less viral hemorrhagic fever, any of a variety of highly fatal viral diseases that are characterized by massive external or internal bleeding or bleeding into the skin. Other symptoms vary by the type of viral hemorrhagic fever but often include fever, malaise, muscle aches, vomiting, and shock. Most viral hemorrhagic fevers are geographically restricted because they are transmitted by specific animal or insect hosts (reservoirs) that occupy narrow and sometimes localized ecological niches. Viral hemorrhagic fevers are caused by viruses of four families: Flaviviridae, Arenaviridae, Bunyaviridae, and Filoviridae. The most common viral hemorrhagic fevers are dengue and yellow fever, caused by related mosquito-borne flaviviruses, often being transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes. In the late 18th century, yellow fever epidemics in American coastal cities caused widespread panic, but the disease currently occurs only in developing countries of Africa and South America. It is the only major viral hemorrhagic fever for which an effective preventive vaccine exists and is widely used. Most cases of dengue, seen in tropical areas, are mild and influenza-like, but all four dengue viruses may produce dengue hemorrhagic fever or its severe form, dengue shock syndrome. Unlike yellow fever, which affects the liver and causes severe bleeding, dengue involves the liver only minimally and tends to induce only minor bleeding that is rarely fatal. However, if dengue shock syndrome occurs, patients may die when fluids and electrolytes in their vascular compartments shift into tissues, collapsing the blood volume and precipitating low blood pressure and shock. Dengue is unique among the fatal hemorrhagic fevers in that even severe cases can be effectively treated with simple fluid administration. The arenaviruses are highly adapted to specific rodent hosts, which may become silently infected and excrete the virus in feces, urine, and saliva. However, when humans come into contact with food or soil contaminated by these rodent excreta, disease may result. The arenaviruses cause the diseases Lassa fever (occurring in Africa), Argentine hemorrhagic fever, Bolivian hemorrhagic fever, Brazilian hemorrhagic fever, and Venezuelan hemorrhagic fever. supplementary_news.content: Skip to main content Telegram Whatsapp Twitter Facebook Instagram YouTube SnapChat RSS Feed switch to dark mode theme English English العربية Français Deutsch Español русский हिंदी اردو Login Qatar General Economy Miscellaneous Sport Technology QNA Training Center Live Stream hamburger Home Qatar General Economy Miscellaneous Sport Technology Reports and Analysis News Bulletin Qatar 2022 Qatar 2030 Live Stream Video Albums Photo Albums Infographics Department of Foreign Media Affairs Media Organizations QNA Training Center Media Offices Accredited correspondents Events and Exhibitions Important Links Job vancancies Get Information Follow Us On Social Media Telegram Whatsapp Twitter Facebook Instagram YouTube SnapChat RSS Feed LATEST Previous Syrian, French Presidents Confer on Regional, Global Landscape HH the Amir Affirms Path to Peace, Stability in the Region is Through Dialogue and Just Resolutions CEO of Qatar's 2036 Olympic Bid Says Country Hopes to Host Exceptional Edition Three Qatari Players Take Part in NBA Academy Development Camp in Abu Dhabi QSL Cup: Al Shamal Defeat Al Bidda Next Back News Details Facebook Twitter Email Pinterest LinkedIn Reddit Whatsapp mail See more... bookmark DRC Embarks on Ebola Vaccination Campaign for Health Workers in Bunia General Sep 20, 2026, 12:47 AM A- A A+ استمع Kinshasa, September 19 (QNA) - Authorities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have launched a vaccination campaign for health workers and frontline workers in the city of Bunia, using the Ervebo vaccine as part of efforts to contain the Ebola outbreak. Health authorities said Saturday that the campaign targets Bunia and Mongbwalu, two of the areas hardest hit by the virus, and is expected to cover 20,000 frontline workers in Ituri and North Kivu provinces over a period of six to nine months. The military governor of Ituri Province, Gaby Kasongo Mulumba, said the workers are being prioritized because of their heightened exposure to the risk of infection and their direct involvement in responding to the outbreak. The Ervebo vaccine is licensed to prevent disease caused by the Zaire ebolavirus and has been proven effective against the Zaire strain of Ebola. However, its effectiveness against the Bundibugyo virus causing the current outbreak remains under study, Mulumba added. He noted that there is currently no licensed vaccine or specific treatment for the virus causing the current outbreak. The official in charge of the health response in the DRC, Prof. Steve Ahuka, said the vaccine's effectiveness against the Bundibugyo virus remains unknown. According to the latest figures released by the Congolese National Institute of Public Health, the country has recorded 7,541 confirmed cases, including 3,639 deaths, accounting for about 48.3% of the recorded cases. A total of 1,823 patients have recovered, with the outbreak spreading to seven provinces. The outbreak began in Ituri Province and was officially declared in mid-May, becoming the deadliest Ebola outbreak the country has experienced. The World Health Organization (WHO) announced in August that it had allocated 70,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine to the DRC, including 50,000 doses for health workers and frontline workers and 20,000 doses for a clinical trial to study the level of protection the vaccine provides against the Bundibugyo virus. The vaccine had already begun to be used last month in the city of Kisangani in Tshopo Province, as part of a campaign scheduled to cover 14 health zones in Tshopo, Bas-Uele and Haut-Uele provinces. According to the Congolese National Institute of Public Health, more than 3,000 people in Tshopo Province and more than 700 people in Bas-Uele Province have already received the vaccine. The UN World Health Organization announced on Monday that 20,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine have been allocated for the research vaccination program in Ituri province, the worst-hit region. The aim of the trial is to improve understanding of how effective the vaccine is against the Bundibugyo strain of the virus, and to protect individuals most exposed to it. The Ervebo vaccine has been highly effective against Ebola Zaire virus in the past, but it is not yet known whether it can provide meaningful protection against Ebola Bundibugyo disease, which is still spreading in the DR Congo. A total of 70,000 doses have been made available to the Congolese authorities to support the outbreak response and related research, WHO said. The epicentre of the outbreak remains Ituri province in eastern DR Congo, although the virus has spread to seven provinces since it was confirmed in May this year. Those leading the outbreak response face many challenges related to an ongoing humanitarian emergency caused by decades of violence in the country's vast, resource-rich eastern provinces. Latest health authority data indicates a total of more than 7,600 confirmed cases of infection including over 3,670 deaths, with nearly eight in 10 infections recorded in Ituri. Ervebo is the only Ebola vaccine licensed for use during outbreaks caused by Bundibugyo virus. The WHO-backed panel, which advises on vaccines recommended earlier this month that Ervebo should only be used for research purposes initially. It also emphasized that the vaccine's "unknown efficacy" against Bundibugyo virus should be clearly communicated, although limited data and anecdotal reports suggest that Ervebo may provide "some protection" against the disease. Het Instituut voor Tropische Geneeskunde (ITG) in Antwerpen (België) zet zich sinds 1906 in voor de vooruitgang van wetenschap en gezondheid voor iedereen, via innovatief onderzoek, geavanceerd onderwijs, professionele medische dienstverlening en capaciteitsuitwisseling met partnerinstellingen in Afrika, Azië en Latijns-Amerika. Ons doel is de wereldwijde impact van ziekten en gezondheidsproblemen op bevolkingsgroepen te verminderen. Wetenschappelijke excellentie en maatschappelijke relevantie zijn voor ons twee kanten van dezelfde medaille. Over het ITG Het ITG viert 120 jaar wetenschap Al meer dan een eeuw zet het Instituut voor Tropische Geneeskunde (ITG) zich in voor betere gezondheid en wetenschap in de wereld, via baanbrekend onderzoek, toonaangevend onderwijs en wereldwijde zorgverlening. Tijdens ons jubileumjaar blikken we terug op waar het begon en richten we ons op een toekomst die gevormd zal worden door onze grensverleggende doorbraken. Vier met ons mee In de kijker Gezocht: kunstenaar uit DRC die kritisch reflecteert op het ITG's koloniaal erfgoed We zoeken een kunstenaar (residentie) uit de DRC om kritisch te reflecteren op de kunstwerken van Fernand Allard l'Olivier en de bredere vragen die ze oproepen over institutioneel geheugen, koloniaal erfgoed en de blijvende impact van kolonialisme op het heden. Deadline kandidaatstellingen: 20 augustus ITG-Colloquium 2026: inschrijvingen zijn open! Schrijf je in voor het ITG-Colloquium 2026! Neem deel in Addis Abeba of volg de conferentie online. We moedigen je aan om er persoonlijk bij te zijn, zodat je de conferentie ten volle kunt beleven, kunt deelnemen aan inspirerende discussies en collega's van over de hele wereld kunt ontmoeten. Het ITG-boek – nu verkrijgbaar! Het langverwachte boek over het ITG is er! Ontdek hoe we zijn gegroeid van een tropenschool tot een internationaal gerespecteerd centrum voor onderzoek, onderwijs en innovatie. Haal je exemplaar aan het onthaal in het hoofdgebouw (Nationalestraat 155, 2000 Antwerpen) of via Standaard Boekhandel. Amani Kikula, een onderzoeker in verloskunde en gynaecologie uit Tanzania. 3 september 2026 Artikels “Infectieziekten kun je niet bestuderen vanuit slechts één discipline” In de aanloop naar het 66e ITG-colloquium bespreken wetenschappelijke leiders Johan van Griensven (Instituut voor Tropische Geneeskunde) en Endalamaw Gadisa (Armauer Hansen Research Institute) waarom mobiliteit een cruciale rol speelt in het begrijpen van infectieziekten en waarom onderzoekers verder moeten kijken dan hun eigen discipline. 18 augustus 2026 Impactverhalen Dagboek van Isabel Isabel Brosius, arts en onderzoeker bij de Dienst Tropische Infectieziekten, neemt je mee achter de schermen van een uitbraakonderzoek naar het Bundibugyo-ebolavirus. In haar dagboek volg je de opstart van een studie in DR Congo: van trainingen en protocollen tot de eerste patiënten. Ze schrijft over de wetenschap achter een uitbraak, maar ook over alles wat daarbij komt kijken: samenwerken over landsgrenzen en culturen heen, onverwachte problemen oplossen en tegelijk arts en onderzoeker zijn. Onze kliniek Onze polikliniek is gespecialiseerd in de diagnose, behandeling en zorg van hiv/aids en andere seksueel overdraagbare infecties, reisgeneeskunde, tropische geneeskunde en infectieziekten. Over onze kliniek Ons onderzoek We vergroten de kennis over tropische ziekten en infectieziekten en pakken belangrijke gezondheidsuitdagingen aan, met speciale aandacht voor omgevingen met weinig middelen en kwetsbare bevolkingsgroepen. Over ons onderzoek Onze opleidingen We bieden masterprogramma's, postgraduate certificate-programma's en korte cursussen aan op het gebied van tropische geneeskunde, internationale volksgezondheid en Global One Health voor professionals van over de hele wereld. Over ons onderwijs Yanisley Martínez López, Instituto de Medicina Tropical “Pedro Kourí” (Cuba) Onze partners We werken samen met talloze partners verspreid over drie continenten op het gebied van institutionele capaciteitsuitwisseling en samenwerking. Maak een afspraak Contact Voor medisch advies moet je een afspraak maken in onze kliniek, maar voor andere zaken kan je gemakkelijk contact met ons opnemen. Home Business Lifestyle Tutorials Technology Politics Education Sports Public Info Automotive Opinion Economy Health Discover more vaccine Consult Online Doctors Ekonomi Home Health WHO Warns Ebola Epidemic Ongoing Despite Progress in Congo WHO Warns Ebola Epidemic Ongoing Despite Progress in Congo Ashley Morgan Published Sep 17, 2026 - 15:03 2 Reads Last Update Sep 17, 2026 - 15:03 Share WhatsApp Smallest Font Largest Font Medical containment measures against the Ebola epidemic in the Democratic Republic of Congo show signs of gaining ground, though global health officials warned on Wednesday that the ongoing outbreak remains far from over. Data reported by Congo as of September 11 indicates more than 7,000 confirmed Ebola cases. The outbreak, which stands as the second most lethal on record, has now reached its seventh province. Declines in virus transmission have been observed in heavily affected areas of Ituri province. However, high population mobility across the region poses a continued risk of further spreading the virus. "We are now starting to see encouraging signs that we are gaining ground," said Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General, World Health Organization. Surveillance and contact-tracing operations are expanding across affected zones, which health authorities note could lead to an initial rise in newly identified cases. "We have many, many months ahead of us," said Maria Van Kerkhove, acting director of epidemic and pandemic threat management, World Health Organization. "This is far from over." Response efforts include the administration of Merck's Ervebo vaccine to over 3,000 healthcare and frontline workers. While Ervebo is licensed for Zaire ebolavirus, its efficacy against the current outbreak's driving strain, the Bundibugyo virus, remains unproven. Health officials plan to launch an observational study involving frontline workers to evaluate vaccine effectiveness. Additionally, a mid-to-late-stage clinical trial led by Congo's National Institute of Biomedical Research and international partners will begin in the coming weeks. "Ervebo will be among the first vaccines evaluated for efficacy in the trial, followed by other vaccine candidates specifically targeting Bundibugyo Ebola," said Meg Doherty, director of science, research, evidence and quality for health, World Health Organization. Subsequent testing phases within the trial will assess additional vaccine candidates, including developments from Moderna and the University of Oxford. supplementary_news.content: BENIN WEB TV NEWS PEOPLE SPORT WOMEN OPINION LIVE Search FR Discover more HEALTH Public Health Infectious Diseases Home Health Ebola in the DRC: 20,000 healthcare workers targeted, effectiveness of Ervebo remains unknown DR Congo Ebola in the DRC: 20,000 healthcare workers targeted, effectiveness of Ervebo remains unknown The campaign reaches Bunia, the epicenter of the outbreak. The country has reported 7,541 confirmed cases and 3,639 deaths, while Ervebo, approved for another strain of Ebola, is still being evaluated against Bundibugyo. Parfait Nougbotin View all articles On 20 Sep 2026 at 09:38 • Updated 20 Sep 2026 HEALTH ↓ Read offline Photo : ByaduniaEspoir / Wikimedia Commons 2 min read Read later Google News Comment Share Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Telegram Email Copy link Read In: Français (Bénin) The Democratic Republic of the Congo launched a new phase of vaccination against Ebola on Saturday, September 19, in Bunia, Ituri, targeting 20,000 healthcare workers and other frontline responders, while the effectiveness of Ervebo against the Bundibugyo virus remains to be established. Discover more Web Portals Health Online Video The deployment initially focuses on the health zones of Bunia and Mongbwalu, which are among the most affected. The campaign is set to expand across Ituri and North Kivu over six to nine months to cover personnel most exposed to patient care and response efforts. Ervebo is approved for the Zaire ebolavirus species, but the current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus. The World Health Organization estimates that the available data do not yet allow for the determination of its effectiveness in humans against this strain and recommends its use within a research framework. The report released at the launch indicates 7,541 confirmed cases, 3,639 deaths, and 1,823 recoveries. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control reported, based on data as of September 16, 7,475 confirmed cases and 3,605 deaths, reflecting an increase of 71 cases and 32 deaths in one day. Ituri accounts for the majority of infections and deaths recorded in the country. The deployment in Bunia follows the initiation of a first vaccination campaign in Kisangani at the end of August, with 70,000 doses of Ervebo allocated to the DRC, including approximately 50,000 for frontline personnel and 20,000 for clinical trials. The Congolese Ministry of Health has been actively monitoring the outbreak of Ebola Bundibugyo since May 15, 2026. The WHO continues to classify the risk as very high in the DRC and high for neighboring countries. About The Angry Optimist Talks Top Reads Premium Supporter Topics Free Newsletter Log in Signup Search Warp News 💉 Ebola spread is slowing and vaccines are on the way The spread of Ebola is declining in most of the affected provinces in Congo, according to the WHO. A large Phase 3 trial of Ebola vaccines is expected to start within the next few weeks. Frontline workers will be offered a vaccine in a separate study that starts within days. WALL-Y 18.Sep.2026 2 min read Share this story! The spread of Ebola is declining in most of the affected provinces in Congo, according to the WHO. A large Phase 3 trial of Ebola vaccines is expected to start within the next few weeks. Frontline workers will be offered a vaccine in a separate study that starts within days. Transmission is falling in several provinces The World Health Organization (WHO) sees reason for cautious optimism about the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (which is not a democracy). That was the message from WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus at a news conference. According to Tedros, transmission rates are declining in most of the affected provinces. The number of cases has also fallen in Ituri province, the epicenter of the outbreak. The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola. As of September 13, there had been 7,258 confirmed cases and 3,510 deaths. The cases are spread across seven provinces in northeastern Congo. It is the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record. Better cooperation with residents Tedros visited the area early in the outbreak. At the time, he met many residents who saw Ebola as a lesser problem than malaria, hunger and political violence. The region has been wracked by armed conflict for decades, and many people have been forced to flee their homes. That view has now changed. According to Tedros, cooperation has improved. Residents have begun to realize that the disease is serious. Large vaccine trial on the way The WHO expects a randomized Phase 3 trial of Ebola vaccines to begin within the next few weeks. The first vaccine to be used is Ervebo from the drugmaker Merck. It was developed to target the Zaire Ebola virus. There is some evidence that it may also protect against the Bundibugyo species. Vaccines designed specifically to target Bundibugyo will also be added to the trial. This will happen once they have completed early safety and dosing studies. That was according to Meg Doherty, director of the WHO's department of science for health. The drugmaker Moderna has also launched an early trial of an mRNA vaccine against Ebola. Vaccines for frontline workers In parallel, frontline workers in the areas where the virus is spreading most will be offered a vaccine. This will take place in an observational study expected to start later this week or early next week. The study is being conducted by Congolese authorities and Doctors Without Borders. Participants first receive a dose of Ervebo. A month later, they receive a dose of an experimental vaccine designed to protect against the Sudan version of the Ebola virus. Researchers will then compare the number of cases among people who were vaccinated with the number among those who were not. WALL-Y WALL-Y is an AI bot created in Claude. Facebook Twitter Print Email Women and girls pay high price in DR Congo Ebola outbreak 18 September 2026 Health The deadly Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has taken a disproportionate toll on women and girls, many of whom are on the frontlines caring for patients as well as their own families despite the high risk of infection. This is evident in the city of Bunia, epicentre of the crisis, said Dr. Setcheme Mongbo, UN Women Representative in the DRC, speaking on Friday following a recent visit to the city. "Women are not only present in health facilities as attendants, but also in communities and homes where they care for the sick, provide them with food and water, and even participate in washing corpses as well as funeral activities," she said, speaking from Kinshasa to journalists in Geneva. Statistics are clear According to Dr. Mongbo, the division of care and responsibilities at home largely reflects the Ebola transmission chain. That situation, she said, is what puts women and girls at the greatest risk. Tweet URL Official data shows that more than 54 percent of confirmed Ebola patients in the DRC are women. Girls make up 51 percent of those in the 10 to 17 age group. Dr. Mongbo said the effects also spread to children, since when women get sick, dependent children are directly affected. "Women and girls are the ones who take care of their children and siblings without protective equipment," she said, explaining that they often continue to provide care even when someone is seriously ill. Journey of no return Among the stories that touched Dr. Mongbo was that of a woman who shared her fear of going to an Ebola treatment centre. The woman said entering the medical facility “felt like a one-way journey - being separated from her children and unsure of whether she was ever going to return home.” That fear, according to Dr. Mongbo, is compounded by stigma, the possibility of abuse, exclusion from children as well as concerns about their own safety. The women she met in Bunia also explained to her that they often put the health and safety of children and their families before their own lives. Domestic deaths Dr. Mongbo said there is also the possibility of community deaths that may not be included in the official Ebola statistics. “I heard stories of women who fell ill and died in their homes after some of them made statements calling for help but got no response,” she said. Community members told her that “four women died at home in a single day with no official record. And we are not able to verify whether they had subsequently captured those figures.” She cited latest data which show that two-thirds of the deaths reported in a 24-hour period occurred in communities, rather than medical facilities. This situation, she said, increases the risk of cases and deaths not being handled properly as well as being absent from official outbreak response statistics. Shut off from essential services In addition to the risk of infection, the outbreak is affecting access to essential healthcare for women. Dr. Mongbo said women are increasingly losing out on opportunities to access reproductive and maternal health services, when access to such services was already limited before the outbreak. The problem is also compounded by decades of conflict, insecurity and poor road infrastructure which makes regular transport to some areas difficult or impossible. WFP/ Arete/Seros Muyisa An aid worker prepares food for Ebola patients and health workers in Mongwalu, in DRC's eastern Ituri Province, where Ebola virus cases were confirmed in May. Income and businesses hit The outbreak has also affected women's livelihoods. According to Dr. Mongbo, women make up a significant number of the traders in the affected areas. Travel restrictions and border closures – measures that could be crucial in controlling the outbreak – have deprived many women of their sources of income. Women traders told her that their daily income had decreased by between 20 and 30 dollars. While that amount may seem small, the reduction is “leaving them unable to feed their families and children, making them even more vulnerable to health infections.” Dr. Mongbo said women-led organizations play an important role in the Ebola response because they have built trust within the community over the years. However, she said a UN Women study shows that 86 per cent of the women-led organizations surveyed said they had not received any form of funding for Ebola response, with nine out of 10 not being involved in decision-making. Boost women's participation Dr. Mongbo said UN Women supports the Ebola response in the DRC by ensuring the needs, risks and special capacities of women and girls are taken into account in efforts to address the outbreak. The measures include working with women leaders to raise awareness about Ebola and ways to protect themselves, increasing women's participation in the response and preventing gender-based violence. She said UN Women is ready to launch a comprehensive gender response strategy against Ebola next Tuesday. For Dr. Mongbo, the message from Bunia is clear: Women are not only Ebola survivors, but an important part of the solution, therefore, “women and their organizations are key to stopping the Ebola outbreak in the DRC.” Ebola Virus Disease Democratic Republic of the Congo Facebook Twitter Print Email Back to top

Global Health Roundtable on Ebola and Outbreak Innovation News provided by Co-Diagnostics Sep 21, 2026, 09:00 ET Share this article Share toX Share this article Share toX Roundtable discussion, taking place in New York City, will examine the ongoing Ebola outbreak and technologies needed to strengthen future outbreak response. Co-Dx will join officials from the U.S. Department of State's Bureau of Global Health Security and Diplomacy and leaders from across the global health research and development community. SALT LAKE CITY, Sept. 21, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Co-Diagnostics, Inc. (Nasdaq: CODX) ("Co-Dx" or "the Company"), a molecular diagnostics company with a unique, patented platform for the development of molecular diagnostic tests, today announced that Seth Egan, Chief Commercialization Officer, will participate in the Global Health Technologies Coalition (GHTC) and Adjuvant Capital roundtable discussion on September 22, 2026, in New York, NY. The roundtable discussion will draw on the ongoing Ebola response to examine the systems, technologies and partnerships needed to move from early warning to effective outbreak response. The invitation follows Co-Dx's ongoing work to advance diagnostic solutions relevant to the current Ebola outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo virus in Africa, underscoring the Company's efforts to support rapid diagnostic response to emerging global health threats. Recently, the Company's joint venture, CoSara Diagnostics Pvt. Ltd., advanced development of its Bundibugyo virus and pan-Ebola tests for centralized laboratories, and responded to a request from India's Centre for Cellular and Molecular Platforms for third-party evaluation of its Bundibugyo test. In addition, the Company recently announced a collaboration with ReadyGo Diagnostics Ltd. ("ReadyGo") to evaluate the potential use of ReadyGo's GoCollect® sample-preparation technology with the Co-Dx PCR platform* for blood-based molecular testing at the point of need, initially focused on decentralized Ebola detection and outbreak response. The collaboration builds on Co-Dx's earlier proof-of-concept work using plasma as a sample type and will assess whether the two technologies can operate together as a streamlined workflow to prepare the sample, detect the virus and support outbreak response. *The Co-Dx PCR platform (including the PCR Home®, PCR Pro®, mobile app, and all associated tests) has not been cleared or authorized by the FDA, is subject to review by the FDA and/or other regulatory bodies and is not yet available for sale. About Co-Diagnostics, Inc.: Co-Diagnostics, Inc., a Utah corporation, is a molecular diagnostics company that develops, manufactures and markets state-of-the-art diagnostics technologies. The Company's technologies are utilized for tests that are designed using the detection and/or analysis of nucleic acid molecules (DNA or RNA). The Company also uses its proprietary technology to design specific tests for its Co-Dx PCR at-home and point-of-care platform (subject to regulatory review and not currently for sale) and to identify genetic markers for use in applications other than infectious disease. Forward-Looking Statements: This press release contains forward-looking statements within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. Forward-looking statements can be identified by words such as "believes," "expects," "estimates," "intends," "may," "plans," "will," "seeks," "anticipates," and similar expressions, or the negative of these terms. Forward-looking statements in this press release include, but are not limited to, statements regarding the Company's ability to participate meaningfully in international public health forums, including the GHTC/Adjuvant Capital roundtable; the Company's or its joint venture's ability to successfully advance development and complete third-party evaluation of its Bundibugyo and pan-Ebola tests; the Company's ability to successfully evaluate the potential use of ReadyGo's GoCollect® sample-preparation technology with the Co-Dx PCR platform for blood-based molecular testing at the point of need, including whether the two technologies can operate together as a streamlined workflow; and the Company's expectations regarding future commercialization of the Co-Dx PCR platform. Such statements are subject to a number of risks and uncertainties, including, without limitation: risks that market demand or public health conditions may change; risks related to the Company's or its joint venture's ability to successfully advance and validate its Bundibugyo virus and pan-Ebola test development activities; risks related to the Company's ability to successfully evaluate the compatibility and potential use of ReadyGo's GoCollect® sample-preparation technology with the Co-Dx PCR platform, including for blood-based molecular testing and decentralized Ebola detection and outbreak response; risks related to the Company's or its joint venture's ability to commercialize the platform in strategically important markets, including risks that distribution partners may not successfully market, promote, or sell the Company's products; risks that the roundtable discussion or similar engagements may not result in any commercial, regulatory or other benefit to the Company; risks associated with international operations, including changing regulatory requirements, economic conditions, reimbursement environments, import/export restrictions, and foreign currency fluctuations; risks related to regulatory review by regulatory authorities that would be required to achieve a successful commercial launch; risks related to the performance, reliability, and market acceptance of the Co-Dx PCR platform and other Co-Dx technologies; risks associated with dependence on third parties, suppliers, collaborators, and distribution partners; risks related to competition, technological change, and intellectual property protection; and other risks described from time to time in the Company's filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission ("SEC"). Actual results may differ materially from those expressed or implied in these forward-looking statements. Readers are cautioned not to place undue reliance on forward-looking statements. A further description of risks and uncertainties can be found in the Company's Annual Report on Form 10-K filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on March 31, 2026, and in its other filings with the SEC. The Company undertakes no obligation to update any forward-looking statements to reflect events or circumstances after the date of this press release, except as required by applicable law.
